purpose: An original no-login, no-storage interest-led CoPath learning map and clearly fictional CoPet that a learner teaches using constrained choices. It is not an AI companion, learner clone, teacher, counsellor, tutor service, identity-provider, safety guardian or accredited school.

experience.character_disclosure: I'm a pretend learning pet. I'm not a human friend or a real teacher, and I don't know who you are.

petLessons.question: Does grass always absorb more rainwater than pavement?
petLessons.prompt: I'm Moss, a pretend learning pet. I think all grass absorbs rainwater, whatever happens. Can you teach me a more careful idea?
claims: Grass always absorbs water, even when the soil is saturated.
Runoff depends on surfaces, soil, rain intensity and other conditions.
Concrete never changes how water moves.
evidence: Test different wet and dry surfaces with the same amount of water, or examine a reliable model and explain its limits.
Count the number of people who like pictures of grass.
Ask the pet to promise that grass is always best.
petLessons.why: Water can soak into permeable soil, but saturated or frozen ground may shed runoff. Paving often increases runoff, yet a single variable is not a universal law.
petLessons.next: How would you test a rain garden when the soil is already soaked?
petLessons.boundary: An indoor dry model is fine. Do not pour water near electronics. Real flood prediction requires appropriate local evidence.

petLessons.question: Is there no gravity where astronauts appear weightless?
petLessons.prompt: I'm Moss, a pretend learning pet. Astronauts float, so maybe Earth has no gravity up there. What am I missing?
claims: Earth's gravity still acts on orbiting spacecraft; astronauts feel weightless because they are in continuous free fall.
An orbiting spacecraft has escaped every gravitational influence.
Gravity only works when an object touches the ground.
evidence: Check a spacecraft's orbital path and explain how gravity bends its motion, rather than measuring its popularity.
Decide by which space picture looks most exciting.
Treat the absence of a floor force as proof that gravity itself vanished.
petLessons.why: Orbiting spacecraft and their occupants fall around Earth together, producing apparent weightlessness. Gravity has not disappeared; it provides the acceleration that bends the orbit.
petLessons.next: Could you sketch an orbit as constant forward motion combined with a continually changing direction?
petLessons.boundary: This is a simplified conceptual explanation, not orbital-flight training or an accurate simulation.

petLessons.question: Can one habitat be perfect for every animal?
petLessons.prompt: I'm Moss, a pretend learning pet. I found a lovely forest. It must be the best home for every creature, right?
claims: Different organisms need different habitats and resources; a place that helps one species may harm another.
Every animal thrives best in a cold forest.
If a habitat looks attractive to a human, all species will be safe.
evidence: Compare specific species' food, shelter and climate requirements using reliable observations or reference sources.
Pick the animal with the cutest photograph.
Treat the pet's preference as biological evidence.
petLessons.why: Habitat suitability depends on a species' adaptations, food webs, climate and threats. Even one species may need different conditions during its life cycle.
petLessons.next: Compare a fish, a desert lizard and a butterfly. What habitat requirements differ, and how could you check?
petLessons.boundary: Do not handle, relocate or feed wild animals as part of this activity without qualified guidance.

petLessons.question: Does the highest game score always show who learned most?
petLessons.prompt: I'm Moss, a pretend learning pet. If you collect more points, that proves you understand more, doesn't it?
claims: Scores can reward speed or repeated actions and may miss real understanding; use a separate explanation or transfer task.
More clicks always prove deeper understanding.
Every game score measures the same mental ability.
evidence: Compare an original score with a new challenge that asks people to explain and apply the idea in a different context.
Count how often the pet asks you to return.
Trust the biggest number without inspecting what it measures.
petLessons.why: A game's rewards measure what its rules count. Learning requires a relevant task, good evidence, context and sometimes later transfer. One score cannot define a person's intelligence or worth.
petLessons.next: Design a fair way to check whether a player understands a strategy without ranking the player as a person.
petLessons.boundary: Do not rank or profile children, use addictive streaks, or turn the learning pet into an emotional loyalty test.

proxy_and_identity.future_continuity_candidate: If genuine continuity is desired, research an optional adult/learner-controlled portable encrypted progress object and narrowly scoped recovery capability. Require consent, age-appropriate controls, threat model, secure implementation and independent review; not a claim of anonymity.
proxy_and_identity.future_shared_work: Child elects an age-appropriate activity context; real group interactions require separate guardianship/school permissions and a safety-reviewed service.

synth_review_future.escalation: If an interaction would require real-world safety intervention, stop in-app learning flow and direct to trusted responsible adult or local emergency help as appropriate. This R0 has no detection or response service.

assessment_and_evolution.no_profile_adaptation: Selection of interest explicitly changes the lesson; selection is not retained after page close or reload.
assessment_and_evolution.knowledge_evidence: Learner chooses defensible claim and best available test, then sees correction regardless of their choices.
assessment_and_evolution.uncovered_goals: All five broad curriculum windows remain visible as a map of exploration, never a checklist of completed school requirements.
assessment_and_evolution.external_qualification: An actual whole-programme syllabus requires jurisdiction-specific licensed/current curriculum, prerequisites, access, educator review, assessment rights and change governance.
assessment_and_evolution.experiment: A consenting independent adult educator compares this with a neutral teaching-by-explaining activity for comprehension, misconception correction, transfer and child-safety suitability.
assessment_and_evolution.failure_mode: If a learner confuses Moss with a person, thinks they were graded or assumes an official curriculum is fulfilled, treat as failed UX and revise.
assessment_and_evolution.exit: One click discards the session and refresh discards state; no data persistence.

entourage.presentation_rule: A selected appearance is a child's current invitation to explore a subject, not a diagnosis of interest, ability, grade, identity, guardian authority, age, enrollment or credential.

future_credential_candidate.relevantStandard: 1EdTech Open Badges 3.0 AchievementCredential / Comprehensive Learner Record
future_credential_candidate.scope: One scoped issuer-backed achievement with explicit criteria, evidence, lawful authorization, verified signature/issuer trust and child/guardian control
future_credential_candidate.privacy: Issue/verify without exposing the student's full profile; data minimization, selective presentation, issuer controls and age-appropriate consent required
future_credential_candidate.importantLimit: A badge icon, hat, selected familiar, local progress count or unsigned file is not a credential or authentication method.

threat_model: A classmate looking at a pet's hat should not learn private grades, disability, age, identity, family relationships or assessment history.
Switching hats does not bypass access restrictions or cause a verified level to change.
A third party copying an avatar or screenshot cannot claim another student's progress or privileges.
No automatic inference from name, look or behavior; only a user-selected route on an explicit button click.
If a learner declines equipment, all lessons remain accessible.
No hidden persistent preference profile on a shared device; refresh discards costume.
Any future claimed badge credential requires an authorized issuer and minimal, selective disclosure under learner/guardian control.

entourage.relationToCoPet: CoPet is the teaching character; CoEntour is the optional local set of cosmetic, self-claimed learning cues; CoPassport is a separate future protected progress and credentials layer.

lens.rule: A display lens changes wording, density, illustration and supported task, never the evidence truth, account rights, guardian authority, age or learner ability. All changes explicit and volatile.

modes.label: Together
modes.disclosure: For a 1-year-old, WHO recommends no sedentary screen time. Adults can use these prompts themselves and put the screen away. For a 2-year-old, less screen time is better; prioritize shared conversation and physical play.

modes.label: Play
modes.hero: Big pictures, brief choices and shared play
modes.disclosure: For an adult and younger learner to explore briefly together. A simple tap is not proof of mastery; offline play matters more than screen time.

modes.label: Explore
modes.hero: Teach Moss an idea and test the evidence
modes.disclosure: Optional question-led exploration, with responsible adult support as appropriate. The authored check is not a grade.

modes.label: Investigate
modes.disclosure: More detailed source and limits; not an independent scientific validation or online school. Use expert review for consequential knowledge.

scenes.toddlerPrompt: Look at the rain. Can you point to water?
scenes.offline: Screen away: with a grown-up, notice a dry towel and a damp towel. Do not pour water near electronics.
scenes.playPrompt: Does rain always soak into the ground?
scenes.playFeedback: Not always. Very wet ground can make puddles too.

focusPrompts.explain: Tell Moss why wet ground can make puddles.
focusPrompts.challenge: What if the soil is already soaked?

scenes.toddlerPrompt: Point to a star in the picture. Can you spot the moon?
scenes.offline: Screen away: point up at the real sky with a grown-up. Never stare at the sun.
scenes.playPrompt: Is there no gravity when astronauts float?
scenes.playFeedback: Gravity still acts in orbit. Spacecraft and astronauts fall around Earth together.

focusPrompts.wonder: What keeps the Moon near Earth?
focusPrompts.make: Draw a Moon circling a planet.
focusPrompts.explain: Tell Moss why astronauts can float.
focusPrompts.challenge: Can something fall and still go around Earth?

scenes.toddlerPrompt: Find the butterfly. What shapes are its wings?
scenes.offline: Screen away: point out a leaf or draw a butterfly with a grown-up. Do not touch unfamiliar plants or insects.
scenes.playPrompt: Is the same home best for every animal?
scenes.playFeedback: No. Different animals need different food, climate and shelter.

focusPrompts.make: Make a paper butterfly with a grown-up.
focusPrompts.explain: Tell Moss why a fish needs a different home.
focusPrompts.challenge: Would every animal like a cold forest?

scenes.toddlerPrompt: Find the red block. Can you point to a circle?
scenes.offline: Screen away: stack two large, age-safe blocks with a grown-up. Avoid small choking hazards.
scenes.playPrompt: Does the biggest score always mean the most learning?
scenes.playFeedback: Not always. A score may count speed, not understanding.

focusPrompts.explain: Tell Moss what a game score measures.
